title: Uru-Eu-Wau-Wau - Wikipedia
text: The Uru-Eu-Wau-Wau people call themselves Jupaú. They are also (mistakenly) known as the Amondauas, Bocas-negras, Bocas-pretas, Cabeça-vermelha, Cautários, Sotérios, Urupain, [1] as well as Jupaú, Black-Mouths, Red-Heads, Urueu-Wau-Wau.

title: Uru-Eu-Wau-Wau dialect - Wikipedia
text: Uru-Eu-Wau-Wau (Uru-Eu-Wau-Wau: Jupaú) is one of the eight varieties of the Kagwahiva language, a Tupi–Guarani language, Subgroup VI. [2] The name is also spelled Uru-Eu-Uau-Uau, Eru-Eu-Wau-Wau and Ureuwawau, and is sometimes known simply as Kagwahiva.

title: Uru-Eu-Wau-Wau — Grokipedia
text: The Uru-Eu-Wau-Wau, self-identified as the Jupaú meaning "those who use jenipapo," are a small indigenous ethnic group belonging to the Tupi-Guarani linguistic family, inhabiting the Uru-Eu-Wau-Wau Indigenous Territory in the state of Rondônia, Brazil. [1]

title: Amundava Language (Amondawa and Uru-Eu-Wau-Wau tribes)
text: The language of a neighboring Tupian tribe, Uru-eu-wau-wau (or Jupau) is so closely related to Amundava that many linguists consider them dialects of a single language.
